The provided text does not contain any information regarding John von Neumann. The document is a compilation of biographies for Charles Sanders Peirce, Garry Kasparov, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Bertrand Russell, John von Neumann, and Noam Chomsky.
However, based strictly on the section titled "John von Neumann" within the text, here is a summary of his life and work:
John von Neumann (1903–1957) was a child prodigy from a wealthy Jewish family in Hungary who became one of the most influential mathematicians and scientists of the 20th century. He earned degrees in both chemistry and mathematics, graduating *summa cum laude* from ETH Zurich and the University of Budapest in 1926, before studying under David Hilbert at the University of Göttingen. His academic career included positions at the University of Berlin, Princeton University, and the Institute for Advanced Study, where he was elected a Privatdozent at age 23, making him the youngest in the university's history. He married twice; first to Marietta Kövesi (1930–1937), with whom he had a daughter, and later to Klára Dán (1938–1957), who assisted in programming early computers.
Von Neumann made foundational contributions to numerous fields. In mathematics, he axiomatized set theory, developed ergodic theory, and established the theory of operator algebras and functional analysis. In physics, his 1932 work, *Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics* , provided a rigorous mathematical framework for the field, introducing concepts such as the density matrix and von Neumann entropy, though he later felt his work on the measurement problem regarding the role of consciousness was incomplete. In economics, he founded game theory with Oskar Morgenstern and proved the minimax theorem, while also contributing significantly to mathematical economics through models of expanding economies and linear programming.
In computer science, von Neumann is a founding figure known for designing the stored-program architecture (the basis of the "von Neumann architecture") used in most modern computers, inventing the merge sort algorithm, and developing cellular automata and the theory of self-reproducing automata. He also pioneered scientific computing, numerical analysis, and the Monte Carlo method. His extensive defense work included leading the mathematics of shaped charges for the Manhattan Project (designing implosion lenses for the Fat Man bomb) and serving as a key advisor to the U.S. military on the development of ICBMs and the hydrogen bomb. He died of cancer in 1957 at age 53, shortly after his death, the Soviet Union's first ICBM was successfully tested.
